claims.claim: Planar two-exit instances admit a cyclic two-gate decomposition. Let the exits be p,q and let B=N(p)∩N(q). Every component of G−({p,q}∪B) is adjacent to at most two vertices of B; when |B|≥3, those two are consecutive in the cyclic order of B around the exits.
claims.evidence: Fix a plane embedding and retain the K_{2,|B|} subgraph on {p,q}∪B. For |B|≥3 it is 2-connected, with |B| faces by Euler's formula. Its facial boundaries are cycles of length at least four, while their total length is 4|B|, so every face is exactly p-b_i-q-b_{i+1}-p. A connected component disjoint from this skeleton lies in one face and can therefore meet only its two consecutive B-vertices. For |B|≤2 the bound is immediate.
claims.witness: Each remainder component lies in a face bounded by p-b_i-q-b_{i+1}-p.
claims.search_method: Independent plane-embedding proof, supplemented by exhaustive inspection of every planar labeled graph through six vertices; no component with more than two gates occurred.

claims.claim: There is a linear-time classification when the exits have the same independent neighborhood. After deleting a possible irrelevant edge pq, suppose N(p)=N(q)=B and B is independent. The fugitive wins exactly when (i) s∈{p,q}∪B, (ii) s has a neighbor in B, or (iii) s has a neighbor w having two distinct neighbors in B.
claims.evidence: Conditions (i) and (ii) give immediate escape, while in (iii) the two three-edge gate configurations are edge-disjoint, so one Nemesis deletion cannot spoil both. Conversely, if all conditions fail, after the first move to w its outside component has at most two boundary gates and w sees at most one. Nemesis prepares such a gate by deleting one exit edge. Maintain the invariant that any unprepared boundary gate is not adjacent to the current outside vertex; when it first becomes adjacent, the intervening move gives Nemesis time to prepare it. On entry into a prepared gate, Nemesis deletes its other exit edge. Independence of B forces the next non-exit move into an outside component whose boundary consists of the dead gate and at most one new gate, restarting the invariant. Finite edge deletion then forces a Nemesis win. All tests are adjacency scans.
claims.witness: The exact enumeration tested 7,010 promised graph/start cases through six vertices and found zero classifier mismatches.
claims.search_method: Bidirectional strategy proof plus exhaustive exact minimax testing of all promised planar instances through six vertices.

claims.claim: Two broader target-relevant subclasses are linearly solvable: (a) the graph induced by regular vertices is a forest, with arbitrary degrees; or (b) every regular vertex has degree at most three, with arbitrary exit degrees.
claims.evidence: Replacing each regular-exit incidence by its own pendant exit preserves every regular move, relevant deletion, terminal exit move, and the property of being connected to an exit. In case (a), the transformed start component is a tree; in case (b), every transformed vertex has degree at most three. The source's linear algorithms therefore apply, and the incidence replacement has linear size.
claims.witness: After exit splitting, the regular core is unchanged and all new vertices are degree-one exits.
claims.search_method: Checked the state-by-state reduction in both directions and its degree/acyclicity consequences; the checker additionally exhausts the correspondence through five vertices.

claims.claim: Internal-edge deletions are essential even for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits: constraining Nemesis to delete only exit-incident edges can change the winner. Let the exits be p,q, the start be s, and the other vertices be x,a,b, with edges pa,pb,qa,qb,ax,xs,ab. Nemesis wins the original game, but the Fugitive wins under that restriction.
claims.evidence: In the original game, s→x is forced and deleting xa immediately separates x from both exits. Under exit-incident-only deletion, if the first deletion damages b, both a-exit edges remain; if it damages a, the Fugitive enters a and either exits there or, after both a-exit edges are removed, traverses ab to the still-fresh b. One later deletion cannot block both b-exit edges.
claims.witness: The exact solver returned Fugitive=false in the original game and Fugitive=true under the restriction; the integer-coordinate drawing was also crossing-free.
claims.search_method: Exact minimax recurrence and integer orientation/segment-incidence tests.

claims.claim: Nemesis is not invariant under edge subdivision, even on planar simple trees with exactly two exits. With exits p,q, start s, and regular vertex a, the graph with edges sa,ap,aq is a Fugitive win, while subdividing sa once with a new regular vertex x makes it a Nemesis win. More generally, replacing r parallel sa edges by the r paths s-x_i-a fails to preserve the winner for every r≥1.
claims.evidence: In the unsubdivided graph, s→a leaves at least one of ap,aq after a single deletion. In the subdivided graph, after s→x Nemesis deletes xa and traps the Fugitive. For general r, whenever the Fugitive enters an uncut x_i from s, Nemesis deletes x_i a; after a return to s or entry into an already cut branch, she deletes another surviving x_j a. Thus a is never reached and all r forward edges are eventually removed. K_{2,r} with leaves p,q is simple and planar.
claims.witness: The r=1 pair consists of the claimed four- and five-vertex planar trees; exact evaluation also confirmed original=true and subdivided=false for every r from 1 through 6.
claims.search_method: General invariant proof plus exact multiedge/simple-bundle minimax checks.

claims.claim: The binary-escape-tree condition is not necessary even for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits. A seven-vertex counterexample has exits p,q, start s, regular vertices a,b,c,z, and edges pa,pb,qa,qb,ab,az,bz,bc,cz,cs.
claims.evidence: After s→c, if bc is deleted, c→z leaves two edge-disjoint gate configurations through a and b, so one further deletion cannot spoil both. Otherwise c→b; if an exit edge at b survives, escape is immediate, while deletion of both bp,bq uses the first two deletions and leaves b→a with both a-exit edges intact. After exit splitting and pruning, only s and c can be roots within distance one. Vertex s has degree one. A tree rooted at c cannot use regular leaf s, so its children must be b,z; then z would require both a and the already-used b as children, creating a cycle. Hence the tree condition fails.
claims.witness: Exact evaluation returned Fugitive=true, tree-condition=false, and verified the supplied straight-line drawing using integer predicates.
claims.search_method: Explicit game strategy, exhaustive binary-tree subgraph test after exact source preprocessing, and integer planarity checks.

claims.claim: The seven-vertex binary-escape-tree counterexample is vertex-minimal: no planar simple Nemesis instance with exactly two exits and at most six vertices has a Fugitive-winning regular start that fails the binary-escape-tree condition after the source's exit splitting and pruning.
claims.evidence: Independent enumeration fixed exits 0,1 and covered every edge subset for n=3,4,5,6 and every regular start. For at most six vertices, Kuratowski's theorem makes the implemented planarity filter complete: only K5, K5 with one subdivided edge, and K3,3 can occur as forbidden subdivisions. The audit retained 33,166 planar labeled graphs and 125,655 exit-connected regular starts. Of 111,587 Fugitive wins, none failed the tree condition after exact exit splitting, iterative pruning, and exhaustive candidate-tree testing. A separately phased game evaluator agreed on all 125,655 starts.
claims.witness: Boundary totals were 111,587 winning starts and zero tree-condition failures; the seven-vertex graph from claim 5 supplies the matching upper witness.
claims.search_method: Complete deterministic enumeration with two independently structured exact game evaluators and exhaustive transformed-tree recognition.

claims.claim: An exact recurrence gives PSPACE membership and an O*(8^n) planar algorithm, although not a polynomial classification. For deleted-edge set D and current regular vertex v, W(D,v) holds iff some surviving move vw reaches an exit or, for every surviving edge e Nemesis might delete, w remains connected to an exit and W(D∪{e},w) holds.
claims.evidence: The precise scope is ∃ surviving vw [w is an exit ∨ ∀ surviving e (w remains exit-connected in G−(D∪{e}) and W(D∪{e},w))], matching the Fugitive move followed by every possible Nemesis response. Every recursive call adds one deleted edge. Depth-first evaluation therefore uses polynomial space. Memoization has at most n·2^m states and polynomial work per state; for a simple planar graph m≤3n−6, this is O*(2^m)=O*(8^n).
claims.witness: The recurrence and an evaluator with separate Fugitive-turn and Nemesis-turn states agreed on all 125,655 exit-connected starts through six vertices.
claims.search_method: Direct quantifier/timing derivation, state-space analysis, and exhaustive cross-check against an independently phased evaluator.

target_evidence: The draft does not give a polynomial-time algorithm or matching hardness result for all planar simple graphs with exactly two exits, and it explicitly labels itself partial. It nevertheless establishes correct structural decomposition, a nontrivial promised-case classification, two broader linear-time subclasses, sharp small obstructions, a verified seven-vertex minimality result, and an exponential/PSPACE baseline directly relevant to the open target.
